title: DeciCAD: Harness-Grounded Learning of Action Policies for CAD Agents
title_zh: DeciCAD：基于智能体框架的 CAD 智能体动作策略学习

paragraphs.en: Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness. We investigate how this operating space shapes agent behavior and policy learning in computer-aided design (CAD), a professional domain characterized by persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures. We instantiate this perspective in DeciCAD , a domain-native harness that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions. Building on this harness, we develop a learning pipeline that extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories and improves the policy through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL). Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves the best F1 and intersection over union (IoU) while reducing model-output tokens by 45–88% relative to a general-purpose coding harness. Under matched supervision, its SFT policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms the coding policy; subsequent online RL further raises geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5% and F1 to 0.7880. These results demonstrate that the decision space induced by a harness materially affects both agent execution and policy learning in CAD.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as agents to operate professional software and complete long-horizon tasks ( Achiam et al. 2023 ; Naveed et al. 2025 ; Guo et al. 2024 ) . Computer-aided design (CAD) is a particularly demanding setting for such agents ( Willis et al. 2020 ; Wu et al. 2021 ) . Unlike one-shot content generation, CAD modeling requires a sequence of state-dependent operations over a persistent design document. An agent must create and modify sketches, constraints, features, and geometric objects; inspect intermediate results; recover from execution failures; and maintain references across long interaction trajectories. In this process, the model outputs are interpreted as actions: each action changes the current CAD state, produces execution feedback, and conditions the next decision ( Yao et al. 2023 ; Schick et al. 2023 ) . The effectiveness of a CAD agent therefore depends not only on the underlying model and its reasoning strategy, but also on how CAD actions, states, and execution outcomes are represented to the model.

Such a model–environment boundary is defined by an agent harness ( Yang et al. 2024 ) . In CAD, a harness determines which design operations the model can express, which parts of the evolving design state it can inspect, and how execution outcomes are returned for subsequent decisions. A general-purpose coding harness may expose the CAD system through programs, libraries, and runtime feedback, whereas a domain-native harness may expose structured CAD actions and object-level observations. Consequently, even when the model, task, and CAD backend remain fixed, different harnesses can present the model with substantially different decision spaces, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Existing work has studied CAD code generation, tool-using agents, execution repair, and interactive modeling ( Mallis et al. 2024 ; Guan et al. 2025 ; Doris et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ; Barkley et al. 2026 ; Gong et al. 2026 ) , but the harness itself is typically treated as implementation infrastructure rather than as a variable that shapes both agent execution and policy learning. This raises a central question: How should a CAD agent harness represent actions and states so that it preserves the decisions required for complex modeling while avoiding representation burden that is irrelevant to the task?

This trade-off is important in CAD. A fine-grained coding interface gives the model broad control over the underlying software, but the same CAD operation can often be expressed through many programs, command sequences, variable names, temporary objects, and API combinations. These implementations may produce the same geometric state transition, but they appear as different generation and supervision targets. The model must then spend capacity on implementation choices that do not affect the intended state transition. A semantic interface can remove many of these choices by representing the intended operation directly. However, excessive compression can hide state differences that require different actions or remove operations needed for correct modeling and error recovery. A useful harness must therefore reduce irrelevant representation choices while preserving the actions and observations needed for correct decisions.

To make this trade-off explicit, we formalize the model-facing interface as a Harness-Induced CAD Decision Space : a harness maps model outputs to executable operations, maps internal CAD states to model-visible observations, and returns execution results as feedback, thereby determining which operations the agent can perform, which state differences and failures it can identify, and which policies it can execute and learn. We then introduce the Semantic Decision Bottleneck as a design principle for this space: it compresses behaviorally equivalent implementations and removes state information that does not affect the next decision, while preserving the actions and observations needed to reach the target geometry and recover from errors.

Following this principle, we develop DeciCAD , a domain-native harness for closed-loop CAD agents. DeciCAD represents task-relevant design transitions as semantic CAD actions, grounds these actions in a persistent CAD document, and returns structured execution feedback together with decision-oriented observations. We further develop a harness-grounded learning pipeline that reconstructs causally conditioned action supervision from successful and recovered interaction trajectories, initializes CAD action policies through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and supports online reinforcement learning (RL) using policy-generated trajectories and geometry-grounded rewards. Figure 2 summarizes this execution and learning loop.

Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD consistently produces more accurate final geometry than competitive CAD agents and a general-purpose coding harness, while reducing model-output tokens by 45–88% relative to the coding harness on text-to-CAD tasks. Observation ablations show that showing more CAD state does not always help: unfiltered state inflates the input context, and coarse feedback strips out what the agent needs in order to recover. With matched training settings, open-weight models trained in the DeciCAD decision space learn stronger long-horizon CAD action policies than the same models trained through code-level interaction.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We define the Harness-Induced CAD Decision Space and introduce the Semantic Decision Bottleneck as a design principle for CAD agent interfaces. We design DeciCAD , which combines semantic CAD actions, compact observations, structured feedback, and persistent object state.

We develop a harness-grounded policy-learning pipeline that reconstructs causally conditioned supervision from interaction trajectories, initializes policies through SFT, and supports geometry-grounded online RL.
Experiments across four benchmarks verify DeciCAD improves geometric accuracy, token efficiency, error recovery, and long-horizon policy learnability significantly.

Our work connects agent interaction interfaces, decision-preserving abstraction, and policy learning in interactive CAD environments. We review these directions through the common question of how an agent’s operating representation affects execution and learning.

Tool-augmented language models connect generation to executable operations ( Parisi et al. 2022 ; Karpas et al. 2022 ; Schick et al. 2023 ) , while API-Bank, Gorilla, and ToolLLM extend tool learning to executable dialogues and large API ecosystems ( Li et al. 2023 ; Patil et al. 2023 ; Qin et al. 2024 ) . ReAct interleaves reasoning, actions, and observations ( Yao et al. 2023 ) ; SWE-agent, WebArena, and OSWorld further show that interaction design affects behavior in stateful coding, web, and computer environments ( Yang et al. 2024 ; Zhou et al. 2024 ; Xie et al. 2024 ) . They establish the empirical importance of interfaces, but generally treat them as tool provision or runtime infrastructure. We instead study the harness as the joint action–state representation that defines the policy space presented to the model.

This view is related to abstraction in sequential decision-making. MDP homomorphisms and state-abstraction theory characterize when compressed representations preserve transition, reward, value, or policy structure ( Ravindran and Barto 2003 ; Li et al. 2006 ; Abel et al. 2016 ; Abel et al. 2020 ) ; the Information Bottleneck similarly retains target-relevant information while suppressing irrelevant input dependence ( Tishby et al. 2000 ) . Classical abstractions operate within an already specified decision process. An LLM harness instead jointly defines model actions, visible observations, execution bindings, and feedback semantics. Our Harness-Induced Decision Space describes this transformation, and the Semantic Decision Bottleneck constrains its compression by decision preservation.

CAD generation has been studied through construction sequences, executable programs, and interactive actions. DeepCAD and Fusion 360 Gallery represent structured modeling histories ( Wu et al. 2021 ; Willis et al. 2020 ) , while Text2CAD and CADmium learn parametric command sequences from language ( Khan et al. 2024 ; Govindarajan et al. 2026 ) . CAD-Coder systems generate executable CAD code ( Guan et al. 2025 ; Doris et al. 2025 ) , and CADFusion, CADSmith, and CADDesigner incorporate rendering, execution repair, or multi-agent feedback ( Wang et al. 2025 ; Barkley et al. 2026 ; Fan et al. 2025 ) . Code is expressive, but also makes program organization and API realization part of the model output.

Interactive systems instead place decisions in evolving design state. CAD-Assistant combines a Python interpreter with FreeCAD operations ( Mallis et al. 2024 ) ; ToolCAD trains tool-using CAD agents from demonstrations and online curriculum learning ( Gong et al. 2026 ) ; CADMate learns sequential assembly actions using geometric and physical rewards ( Chen et al. 2026 ) . Our contribution is complementary: under fixed models, tasks, and terminal geometry, we compare the decision spaces induced by domain-semantic actions and a general-purpose coding harness.

Tool policies commonly acquire initial capability from generated or curated demonstrations ( Schick et al. 2023 ; Li et al. 2023 ; Qin et al. 2024 ) . In a stateful environment, however, action validity depends on the preceding trajectory and feedback; imitation therefore encounters distribution shift when student-induced states depart from teacher trajectories ( Ross et al. 2011 ) . Online methods address this gap using execution outcomes on states visited by the learned policy ( Feng et al. 2025 ; Qian et al. 2025 ) , including curriculum reinforcement learning in CAD ( Gong et al. 2026 ) . We align causal supervision, student rollouts, and environment feedback within the same Harness-Induced Decision Space, enabling a controlled study of how representation affects both imitation and online learning.

The harness determines how the closed CAD loop is presented to the language model: whether the model writes general-purpose code or selects a semantic CAD action, which part of the current design is shown, and how execution failures are reported. We formalize this interaction, formulate the Semantic Decision Bottleneck, instantiate it in DeciCAD , and use the same representation for SFT and online RL.

The distinction is important. A coding harness and DeciCAD may call the same CAD kernel yet induce different sequential prediction problems. Action and observation sufficiency specify what a harness must preserve, but do not uniquely determine its model-facing representation. Among decision-sufficient interfaces, we prefer those that reduce unnecessary burden on both model output and input. We refer to this principle as the Semantic Decision Bottleneck : compressing action representations and visible context while retaining the distinctions required for correct action selection and error recovery. DeciCAD instantiates this principle through domain-specific action schemas, concise execution feedback, and targeted inspection operations that retrieve additional state only when needed. A formal preference relation over decision-sufficient harnesses is provided in the appendix.

These actions express design intent such as sketch and constraint editing, parametric features, Boolean operations, transformations, inspection, and artifact persistence ( Willis et al. 2020 ; Wu et al. 2021 ; Mallis et al. 2024 ) . Using these transitions as the policy-action unit removes distinctions caused solely by program organization, variable naming, or API expansion, while typed parameters and state preconditions retain the information needed for execution.

The binding map β ℋ \beta_{\mathcal{H}} resolves each domain action against the CAD document that exists at that moment and invokes the corresponding backend transition. All accepted actions modify the same persistent document, and stable model-visible identifiers let later actions refer to previously created entities. If parsing, reference resolution, precondition checking, or backend execution fails, the harness keeps the document recoverable and reports the failure. Action semantics are thus grounded in actual CAD transitions rather than textual well-formedness alone.

The response indicates whether the action executed, which objects were modified, which postconditions hold, and where a failure occurred. When more information is needed, inspection actions retrieve object hierarchy, constraints, parameters, dependencies, local measurements, or terminal artifacts.

A complete state dump repeatedly injects irrelevant context; overly generic feedback can instead map states requiring different recovery actions to the same observation. DeciCAD uses compact consequence-related evidence by default and exposes targeted inspection actions so that the policy acquires additional evidence only when the next decision requires it. Later feedback, actions, and terminal evaluation never enter the input, preserving causal conditioning in sequential imitation ( Ross et al. 2011 ; Qin et al. 2024 ) . Recovered failures are retained because their error state, feedback, and corrective action provide genuine CAD recovery supervision.

Uniform decision sampling would overweight long trajectories, repeated inspection, and frequent operations. We therefore stratify causal decisions by task difficulty, design stage, preceding execution outcome, and target action type, preserving modeling, inspection, and recovery decisions under their original histories.

SFT covers teacher-visited CAD states, whereas closed-loop execution reaches states induced by student actions. We therefore sample current-policy rollouts by the same harness and optimize groups containing evaluable terminal geometry. Geometry quality supplies the primary group-relative signal; execution and protocol evidence describe the trajectory but cannot make an all-failure group trainable. Reference-regularized Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with curriculum sampling instantiates this update ( Bengio et al. 2009 ; Shao et al. 2024 ; Qian et al. 2025 ; Gong et al. 2026 ) ; reward coefficients, sampling schedules, and optimizer settings are deferred to the appendix.

Our evaluation follows the methodological chain developed above. We ask whether a semantic CAD decision space preserves the capabilities required for complex modeling, whether its benefits are associated with lower task-irrelevant representation burden, and whether different harness-induced policy spaces exhibit different finite-data learnability and online improvement.

We evaluate harness-level capability, in increasing calibrated difficulty, on CADPrompt ( Alrashedy et al. 2025 ) , a hard subset of CADInstruct ( Lv and Bao 2025 ) , and two P3D-derived benchmarks: P3D-Text-to-3D from Text2CAD and the multimodal P3D-Assembly-3D from the Fusion 360 Gallery ( Khan et al. 2024 ; Willis et al. 2020 ) .

We assign each task a calibrated difficulty that combines semantic complexity, reference-mesh complexity, and description ambiguity, and divide each benchmark into seven equal-frequency quantiles Q ​ 1 Q1 – Q ​ 7 Q7 . Quantiles therefore express relative difficulty within a benchmark rather than the same absolute complexity across benchmarks. The full definition and the distribution of each benchmark are given in Appendix D.1 and Figure 10 .

Using identical task inputs and Claude Opus 4.7 ( Anthropic 2026b ) , DeciCAD is compared with zero-shot CadQuery generation, CADSmith, CAD-Assistant, and Claude Code ( Anthropic 2026a ) . We study policy learning on the standard train–test split of Text2CAD/DeepCAD ( Khan et al. 2024 ; Wu et al. 2021 ) , fixing Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team 2026 ) as the student and Claude Sonnet 4.6 ( Anthropic 2026c ) as the teacher in both the Coding and DeciCAD decision spaces. Generated and reference meshes are normalized, center-aligned, and rigidly registered.

We report Chamfer Distance (CD), surface F1, volumetric Intersection over Union (IoU), and Geometry Availability. F1, IoU, and CD are computed over valid assets; Geometry Availability measures the percentage of tasks entering geometric evaluation. Harness-level and ablation tables scale CD, F1, and IoU by 100, whereas policy-learning tables report their original values. These point-set and occupancy-based measures follow established 3D reconstruction evaluation practice ( Fan et al. 2017 ; Mescheder et al. 2019 ) . To measure representation cost, we report model-visible input and generated output tokens averaged per task; provider-specific cache statistics are excluded. Across tables, best results are bold and second best are underlined. Policy learning for both DeciCAD and the coding harness used eight NVIDIA H800 GPUs; complete configurations are provided in the appendix.

Table 1 compares the same frontier model under different CAD representations and interaction mechanisms. DeciCAD matches or exceeds the strongest coding harness in geometric fidelity while producing evaluable assets across all four benchmarks.

To check that this advantage is not driven only by easy tasks, we divide each benchmark into seven calibrated difficulty quantiles and report end-to-end F1, which assigns zero to missing or invalid outputs (Figure 4 ). DeciCAD and Claude Code have similar slopes on CADPrompt and both decline slowly on P3D-Assembly-3D; DeciCAD is flatter on P3D-Text-to-3D, indicating a more stable advantage under complex textual constraints. Across the individual cells, DeciCAD leads 14 of the 28 dataset–quantile combinations and exceeds Claude Code at the hardest quantile of every benchmark, where missing operations and unresolved state ambiguity would be most visible. Semantic CAD actions therefore preserve the transitions needed for complex modeling while supporting more reliable final geometry. The full quantile heatmaps and difficulty distributions are provided in the appendix.
We test both sides of the Semantic Decision Bottleneck: output scaling characterizes action representation, while observation ablations test whether compression preserves decision-relevant state.

Token totals in Table 1 depend on trajectory length, feedback history, and caching, and therefore do not by themselves identify the source of the output reduction. The reduction does not arise from early termination. DeciCAD trajectories may still be long, but each prediction contains an action and its arguments rather than an expanded implementation, which identifies action representation, rather than shortened reasoning, as the source of the efficiency gain.

Table 2 isolates observation sufficiency on P3D-Text-to-3D. More raw state degrades geometry despite increasing context, whereas removing active inspection or coarsening failure semantics hides distinctions needed by subsequent actions. Effective compression therefore retains decision-identifying evidence rather than simply minimizing or maximizing observation volume. Together, both sides support a decision-sufficient space with lower representation burden.

SFT substantially improves the coding policy, showing that the student can acquire program construction, execution, and repair behavior. Under matched supervision, however, the DeciCAD policy produces more evaluable assets and better geometry across all reported metrics. Coding supervision must resolve geometric intent together with program structure, API choice, and implementation form, whereas DeciCAD binds supervision directly to state-conditioned domain actions. The result supports harness-dependent learnability under finite supervision.

Starting from each SFT policy, we sample student rollouts in its own induced decision space, and apply reference-regularized GRPO with geometry-grounded rewards. The student model, task exposure, samples per task, and evaluator are matched. Improvement is judged by the frozen unseen-task evaluation rather than training reward, trajectory length, or token consumption.

Table 4 shows that online feedback improves DeciCAD across availability and all three geometric metrics, whereas the coding policy does not realize the same gains under the matched inference budget, supporting harness-dependent online learnability.

To compare the learning paths, we map the external effects of both harnesses into six shared categories: Construct, Inspect, Recover, Invalid Reference, No Progress, and Persist, and report events per 100 decisions (Figure 6 ). Coding SFT increases Inspect from 51.6 to 72.1 events per 100 decisions, while Construct and Recover both decline. GRPO restores part of the construction and recovery behavior, but No Progress rises from 18.9 to 30.4, showing that more repair attempts do not consistently produce geometric progress. In DeciCAD , SFT reduces Invalid Reference and No Progress from 18.0 and 33.4 to 4.6 and 21.8, and GRPO further reduces them to 2.1 and 8.8 while retaining dense construction behavior. Coding supervision therefore mainly changes execution, inspection, and repair behavior, whereas DeciCAD learning more directly changes CAD state transitions and suppresses interactions that fail to advance the model.

We formalized Harness-Induced CAD Decision Spaces and instantiated the Semantic Decision Bottleneck in DeciCAD through semantic actions, persistent state, and decision-oriented feedback. Across execution, SFT, and online RL, DeciCAD preserves complex modeling capability while reducing irrelevant burden and enabling more learnable and optimizable policies. Together, these findings show that a harness determines both the CAD operations a model can execute and the distinctions its policy must learn, while environment feedback improves that policy within the same decision representation. This establishes harness design as central to CAD agents. Our study has limitations. The harness comparison uses one CAD backend and one frontier model, policy learning uses one student model on one dataset, and mesh-based metrics do not capture editability, constraint satisfaction, or feature-tree validity. Extending the comparison to further backends, models, and CAD-native correctness measures is left to future work.

The theorem clarifies what a model-facing CAD interface must retain. The model does not require direct access to the complete backend state or to every low-level command. It requires an executable representation of an optimal operation whenever one is needed, together with observations that distinguish backend states whenever those states demand incompatible next actions.

The two conditions also describe distinct failure boundaries. If action sufficiency fails at a reachable state, no action exposed by the harness can attain V g , t ∗ ​ ( s ) V^{*}_{g,t}(s) ; increasing model capacity or adding policy data cannot recover an operation absent from the interface. If observation sufficiency fails at a reachable history, the states consistent with that history share no optimal model action. Any policy conditioned only on the visible history must therefore be suboptimal for at least one of them. The resulting expected loss depends on how often the aliased states occur and on the value gap between the chosen and optimal operations.

Missing actions and state aliasing consequently constrain different sides of the harness-induced decision space. The former limits what the policy can execute; the latter limits what it can distinguish. These boundaries determine which action and observation details may be compressed while preserving the optimal CAD policy.

Decision sufficiency specifies what a harness must preserve, but does not uniquely determine how those capabilities are represented to the model. Two harnesses may connect to the same CAD backend and support the same task-level operations while exposing different numbers of implementation choices, different state granularity, and different forms of execution feedback. The Semantic Decision Bottleneck compares these decision-sufficient representations, adapting the compression principle of the information bottleneck to a model-facing action–observation interface ( Tishby et al. 2000 ) .

We call a transformation from harness ℋ 2 \mathcal{H}_{2} to harness ℋ 1 \mathcal{H}_{1} a decision-preserving compression when it satisfies two conditions. On the action side, model actions may be merged only when, at every task-reachable state where they are admissible, their bound backend operations induce the same distribution over next states and the same task reward for every transition of nonzero probability. The compressed harness must also retain an executable representation of every consequence needed to attain Eq. ( 12 ). This removes differences in syntax or implementation without changing a decision-relevant CAD consequence. On the observation side, visible histories may be identified only when all backend states consistent with any of those histories still share an optimal action in the compressed harness. This is precisely the criterion in Eq. ( 15 ), evaluated after the histories are identified. The action condition retains an optimal executable consequence at every task-reachable state, while the observation condition retains a common optimal action for every compressed history. They therefore preserve action and observation sufficiency, respectively.
For decision-sufficient harnesses, we write

if ℋ 1 \mathcal{H}_{1} can be obtained from ℋ 2 \mathcal{H}_{2} through a decision-preserving compression. The relation expresses a representation preference under fixed decision capability: ℋ 1 \mathcal{H}_{1} does not require the model to distinguish action implementations or visible states that are irrelevant to optimal CAD decisions in ℋ 2 \mathcal{H}_{2} .

Decision-preserving compressions can be applied successively: each step retains the action consequences and state distinctions required by Eqs. ( 12 ) and ( 15 ). The relation therefore supports comparing harnesses by removable semantic structure without selecting a particular action syntax or observation format as canonical.

The Semantic Decision Bottleneck is the decision-sufficient frontier of this relation. A harness lies on the frontier when every further semantic compression violates at least one sufficiency condition. Further action compression crosses this frontier when it removes the only representation of an operation required by Eq. ( 12 ). Further observation compression crosses it when the common-action intersection becomes empty, aliasing states that demand incompatible next actions. The relation need not select a unique frontier harness: different action vocabularies or observation organizations may be incomparable while preserving the same optimal CAD capability. The bottleneck is therefore neither a unique interface nor the shortest one in characters or tokens; it is the frontier of semantic compression subject to preserving the optimal decision policy.

Equation ( 16 ) concerns semantic redundancy rather than token count itself. In a language-model interface, redundant action implementations and state descriptions often increase model input or output, so token use provides an observable measure of representation burden. Nevertheless, semantic compression and token compression are not equivalent. We therefore evaluate a harness jointly by task performance, observation ablations, and token consumption. Nor does the relation by itself guarantee easier optimization for every finite model; the matched SFT and online RL experiments in the main text test whether the induced representation improves policy learning in practice.

Different deployment settings may scalarize these objectives using different weights: for example, interactive systems may penalize inspection latency more heavily, whereas resource-constrained deployments may prioritize context and generation length. More broadly, the harness and policy could be optimized jointly, subject to semantic sufficiency constraints. We leave automated exploration of this harness–policy Pareto frontier to future work.

The main text characterizes a decision-sufficient CAD harness through action and observation sufficiency. This section follows an actual modeling decision through DeciCAD to show how these conditions are instantiated. The model first expresses geometric intent in a semantic action space, the harness grounds that intent in the current CAD state, and the environment returns the execution evidence needed for the next decision. Together, these mechanisms determine the CAD policies that the model can learn and execute.

A modeling policy first requires an action vocabulary capable of expressing design intent. DeciCAD represents each model output as a CAD action with geometric arguments. The vocabulary covers documents and artifacts, sketches and constraints, solid features, Booleans and patterns, edge treatments, object placement, assembly, and state inspection. Each action exposes the variables that determine the CAD state transition. An extrusion, for example, specifies its profile, material mode, extent, and direction, while object resolution and CAD API invocation remain within the harness. This feature-oriented organization follows structured construction histories used in parametric CAD corpora while exposing them as executable interaction steps ( Wu et al. 2021 ; Willis et al. 2020 ; Khan et al. 2024 ) .

The following abstract interface summarizes the model-visible action space. Ref<T> denotes a stable environment-generated object reference that subsequent actions can reuse; the expression after -> describes the geometric postcondition returned after execution.

This representation identifies behaviorally equivalent choices of variable names, control flow, and API syntax as the same action, while retaining the parameters that determine geometric outcome. Stable references compose these actions: a sketch can produce a solid feature; that solid can participate in Booleans, transformations, and edge treatments; and parts can enter an assembly and receive constraints. Each action describes a local geometric transition, while an action sequence incrementally constructs the full design. For the task distribution considered in this work, this compositional closure allows long-horizon modeling policies to remain within one semantic action space, instantiating action sufficiency in the main text.

Semantic actions specify what the model can select; state grounding determines what a selection means in the current design. A point, direction, or rotation has a unique geometric meaning only relative to an explicit coordinate frame. DeciCAD therefore interprets all action arguments under a shared spatial contract. Linear quantities use millimeters and angular quantities use degrees. Documents use a right-handed world frame with (+X) right, (+Y) back, and (+Z) up, and rotations follow the right-hand rule. Two-dimensional geometry lies in the right-handed local frame of its sketch, while solid placement explicitly selects world or parent coordinates. System instructions state these rules, typed arguments mark the space of each value, and the execution layer reports authoritative frames read from the actual CAD placement.

The spatial contract fixes the meaning of arguments, while object references fix their targets. Documents, entities, and reusable topological elements have stable identifiers returned by creation or inspection and reused unchanged in later actions. The harness resolves these references in the current document, executes the native CAD operation, and verifies action-specific postconditions. A valid result is committed to the persistent document so that later actions operate on the resulting state; a failed result preserves the previous state or marks the execution outcome as unknown.

Action grounding is therefore more than a lookup from a tool name to a backend function. The shared spatial contract determines parameter semantics, stable references determine the operated objects, and transactions with postcondition checks determine whether an action actually took effect. Every successful action in the model history corresponds to a verified transition in the persistent CAD document. Together, these constraints implement the binding map defined in the main text.

After an action executes, the model must continue from the resulting environment state. Expanding the complete CAD document repeatedly introduces objects and properties irrelevant to the current decision, whereas reporting only call-level success cannot support geometric judgment or recovery. DeciCAD separates these needs: passive execution feedback describes the state transition that just occurred, while active hierarchical inspection retrieves local state needed by the next decision.

The harness returns success or failure after every action. A success response contains affected objects, action-specific postconditions, and the document generation. A failure response contains an error category, the relevant argument or object, and a recovery direction. Invalid input, missing references, geometric failure, conflict, timeout, and unknown outcome remain distinct because they call for different next actions.

For example, a successful extrusion returns its generated feature, owning body, and solid count; invalid arguments identify the responsible field; and an unknown outcome directs the model to inspect the document before acting again. These distinctions determine whether the policy should continue modeling, revise an argument, or first verify state. Passive feedback therefore retains causal evidence for local continuation and recovery while keeping each step compact.

Passive feedback focuses on the action just completed, but later decisions may depend on a broader portion of the design. An edge treatment may require locating topological edges with particular geometry, while an assembly mate may require checking component placement and connectivity. For these cases, InspectList first discovers relevant state. The model selects a bounded collection—such as entities, children, topology, sketch geometry, constraints, dependencies, or assembly interference—and receives stable references with compact summaries through filtering and pagination. InspectGet then reads the canonical detail of one precise reference, including identity, placement or local frame, bounding box, shape or constraint summary, relations, and validity.

The two inspection levels answer, respectively, which objects are relevant to the current decision and what the authoritative state of one target is. A policy can first list the topological edges of a solid, select candidates from their summaries, retrieve exact geometric properties, and reuse the same reference in a fillet action. Separating discovery from retrieval bounds each observation while allowing the model to recover state distinctions that change the next action. Passive feedback and active inspection thereby instantiate observation sufficiency in the main text.

Across this loop, DeciCAD coordinates compression of model-facing actions and observations. Semantic actions merge behaviorally equivalent implementation forms, while the spatial contract, stable references, and execution verification ensure that the compressed actions still denote well-defined CAD transitions. Passive feedback omits the complete internal state, and active inspection restores local distinctions when a decision requires them. Compression therefore remains constrained by action and observation sufficiency.

Together, these mechanisms instantiate the Semantic Decision Bottleneck from the main text. The model generates CAD decisions rather than their expanded implementations and observes state evidence supporting the next decision rather than the full internal representation of the CAD system. Coordinating actions, grounding, and observations in the same closed loop reduces representation burden without removing the decision paths required for task completion and error recovery.

In the concrete code organization, these mechanisms are separated into three connected components. The harness runtime organizes the decision loop across model invocation, action execution, and feedback. An interface-contract layer defines semantic actions, geometric representations, and execution results. A backend execution layer binds those contracts to native operations in a specific CAD system. This organization allows the interaction policy, the model-visible interface, and CAD execution logic to evolve independently. A new CAD backend implements the same action and feedback contracts while preserving the model-facing decision space.

paragraphs.en: We next describe how closed-loop teacher trajectories are converted into causal supervision and how the resulting policies are selected and evaluated.
paragraphs.zh: 接下来我们描述闭环教师轨迹如何被转换为因果监督，以及如何对所得到的策略进行选择与评估。

paragraphs.en: Policy supervision must preserve the decision conditions under which each action was produced. For every teacher action a t a_{t} , we reconstruct the model-visible history h t h_{t} immediately before that action, including the system instruction, task, preceding model actions, tool results, and available tool schema. The target is the teacher’s next coding response or semantic CAD action. When a trajectory contains a local failure, the failure result remains in the history and supervision is applied to the subsequent recovery decision. This causal construction follows the principle that interactive policies must be trained on histories induced by preceding actions rather than on future trajectory information ( Ross et al. 2011 ; Qin et al. 2024 ) .
paragraphs.zh: 策略监督必须保留生成每个动作时的决策条件。 对于每个教师动作 a t a_{t}，我们重建该动作发生之前模型可见的历史 h t h_{t}，包括系统指令、任务、先前的模型动作、工具结果以及可用的工具模式。 监督目标是教师的下一个编码响应或语义 CAD 动作。 当轨迹中包含局部失败时，失败结果会保留在历史中，并且监督应用于随后的恢复决策。 这种因果式构建遵循以下原则：交互式策略必须在由先前动作诱导的历史上训练，而不是基于未来的轨迹信息（Ross et al. 2011; Qin et al. 2024）。

paragraphs.en: Both datasets originate from the official Text2CAD training split. Claude Sonnet 4.6 executes the same tasks independently through the Coding and DeciCAD harnesses, and the resulting assets are evaluated against the same target geometry. Geometry- and protocol-audited trajectories are then expanded into causal decision examples ( Khan et al. 2024 ; Anthropic 2026c ; Qwen Team 2026 ) . The DeciCAD dataset contains 642 audited tasks, divided by task identity into 542 training and 100 development tasks. Each task retains at most 11 regular and three corrective decisions covering initialization, core modeling, inspection, recovery, and artifact persistence. The Coding dataset contains 499 geometry-valid tasks, of which 471 are used for training and 28 for development, yielding 3,651 training targets and 207 development targets; 336 training targets follow an observed execution error.
paragraphs.zh: 两个数据集均来自官方 Text2CAD 训练集划分。 Claude Sonnet 4.6 通过 Coding 和 DeciCAD 两个执行框架独立完成相同任务，生成的资产针对同一目标几何体进行评估。 经几何与协议审计的轨迹随后被扩展为因果决策样本（Khan 等，2024；Anthropic，2026c；Qwen 团队，2026）。 DeciCAD 数据集包含 642 个经过审计的任务，按任务身份划分为 542 个训练任务和 100 个开发任务。 每个任务最多保留 11 条常规决策和 3 条纠正决策，涵盖初始化、核心建模、检查、恢复以及产物持久化。 Coding 数据集包含 499 个几何有效的任务，其中 471 个用于训练、28 个用于开发，共产生 3,651 个训练目标和 207 个开发目标；其中 336 个训练目标伴随有观测到的执行错误。

paragraphs.en: Online RL continues from states induced by the current student. Training tasks serve four roles: completion_frontier tasks frequently fail to form a valid asset; recovery tasks expose locally recoverable failures; quality_frontier tasks complete but admit geometric improvement; and anchor tasks are solved reliably and constrain forgetting. The first stage emphasizes completion and recovery to expand valid-asset coverage. Its policy becomes the frozen parent of a second, geometry-oriented stage. The final second-stage iteration samples 16 tasks—12 quality-frontier, two completion-frontier, and two anchor tasks—with eight rollouts per task. paragraphs.en: Figure 6 in the main text reports policy behavior under six shared categories. Construct creates or modifies geometric implementation; Inspect executes code, reads state, or checks a result; Recover changes action after an explicit failure and restores progress; Invalid Reference and No Progress record invalid targets and repeated non-progress; and Persist saves or exports the terminal asset. paragraphs.en: Figure 13 grounds the aggregate difference in one shared task. Coding SFT produces no completed trajectory. paragraphs.en: Aggregate geometry, behavior statistics, and trajectory-level evidence jointly define the scope of online improvement. GRPO increases valid-asset coverage and reduces invalid references and repeated non-progress, while small features in long-horizon tasks remain limited by terminal reward resolution. F1 and IoU measure surface and volumetric agreement, and CD adds local distance, but feature count, topological correspondence, repeated structures, and constraint relations can still differ under similar terminal scores. We therefore use closed-loop geometry as the primary evidence and the observed behavior and assets to show how improvement forms within each harness decision space.
paragraphs.zh: 聚合几何、行为统计与轨迹层面的证据共同界定了在线改进的范围。 GRPO 提升了有效资产的覆盖率，减少了无效引用和重复的无进展行为，而长程任务中的细小特征仍受限于终端奖励的分辨率。 F1 和 IoU 衡量表面与体积上的一致性，CD 补充了局部距离信息，但在相似的终端得分下，特征数量、拓扑对应关系、重复结构和约束关系仍可能存在差异。 因此，我们以闭环几何作为主要证据，并结合观察到的行为与资产，说明改进如何在每个 harness 的决策空间内形成。

paragraphs.en: DeciCAD is distributed as a terminal-native Agentic CAD application. It organizes model providers, specialized agents, CAD backends, and project resources in one workspace, allowing a user to create, modify, inspect, assemble, and export native CAD documents through natural-language interaction. This section presents the resulting product workflow, its support for long-horizon multi-agent projects, the backend SDK available to developers, and our official FreeCAD integration. Its streamed action–observation loop follows the interaction pattern established by language agents while grounding each domain action in persistent CAD state ( Yao et al. 2023 ; Yang et al. 2024 ) .
paragraphs.zh: DeciCAD 是一款以终端原生形态发布的智能体化（Agentic）CAD 应用程序。 它将模型提供方、专用智能体、CAD 后端与项目资源组织在同一工作区中，使用户能够通过自然语言交互来创建、修改、检查、装配并导出原生 CAD 文档。 本节介绍最终形成的产品工作流、其对长周期多智能体项目的支持、面向开发者的后端 SDK，以及我们的官方 FreeCAD 集成。 其流式传输的动作–观察循环遵循语言智能体所确立的交互模式，同时将每个领域动作锚定在持久的 CAD 状态之上 ( Yao et al. 2023 ; Yang et al. 2024 ) 。

sents.zh: DeciCAD 是一款以终端原生形态发布的智能体化（Agentic）CAD 应用程序。

paragraphs.en: DeciCAD provides native release packages for macOS, Linux, and Windows and uses a managed installer for application updates. Running decicad inside a project opens that directory as the active workspace; decicad --project /path/to/project selects it explicitly. During initial setup, the application configures a model provider and requests trust before accessing project files or CAD resources.
paragraphs.zh: DeciCAD 为 macOS、Linux 和 Windows 提供原生发行包，并使用托管安装程序进行应用更新。 在某个项目目录中运行 decicad 会将该目录打开为活动工作区；decicad --project /path/to/project 则可显式选择它。 在初始设置过程中，应用会配置一个模型提供方，并在访问项目文件或 CAD 资源之前请求信任。

sents.zh: DeciCAD 为 macOS、Linux 和 Windows 提供原生发行包，并使用托管安装程序进行应用更新。

sents.zh: 在初始设置过程中，应用会配置一个模型提供方，并在访问项目文件或 CAD 资源之前请求信任。

paragraphs.en: The composer accepts part modeling, assembly, geometric revision, inspection, and export requests. An @ reference attaches a project resource such as an image or specification, while $ loads an inline CAD skill that supplies task-specific procedures. Slash commands expose runtime controls in the same interface: /model selects the provider, model, and reasoning effort; /backend installs, activates, updates, and checks a CAD backend; and /status summarizes the current runtime and token usage. Figure 14 shows these operations in the terminal interface.
paragraphs.zh: Composer（作曲家）接受零件建模、装配、几何修改、检查和导出请求。 @ 引用可附加项目资源（如图片或规格说明），而 $ 可加载提供任务特定流程的内联 CAD 技能。 斜杠命令在同一界面中提供运行时控制：/model 选择提供商、模型和推理强度；/backend 安装、激活、更新并检查 CAD 后端；/status 总结当前的运行时和 token 使用情况。 图 14 展示了终端界面中的这些操作。

sents.zh: Composer（作曲家）接受零件建模、装配、几何修改、检查和导出请求。

sents.en: Figure 14 shows these operations in the terminal interface.
sents.zh: 图 14 展示了终端界面中的这些操作。

paragraphs.en: Model actions and environment results then appear in temporal order. File and image reads identify the evidence used by the model, skill loads expose the selected domain procedure, and CAD calls report their execution state and compact result. Successful calls immediately update the persistent document; failed calls return information that supports argument correction, targeted inspection, or selection of another action. The user can interrupt execution or add a follow-up request at any point, and subsequent actions continue from the current CAD state rather than regenerating the artifact from scratch.
paragraphs.zh: 随后，模型动作与环境结果按时间顺序依次呈现。 文件和图像读取用于标识模型所使用的证据，技能加载用于展示所选的领域流程，而 CAD 调用则报告其执行状态和精简结果。 成功的调用会立即更新持久化文档；失败的调用则返回有助于修正参数、进行针对性检查或选择其他动作的信息。 用户可以在任意时刻中断执行或追加后续请求，且后续动作会从当前 CAD 状态继续，而不是从头重新生成产物。

paragraphs.en: The resulting artifact is also available in the native CAD application. Users can inspect the three-dimensional view and access the created Body, Sketch, Feature, Assembly, and Component objects in the document tree. The document can be saved in its native editable format or exported as a standard geometry asset, preserving a path from agent generation to manual inspection and continued engineering work.
paragraphs.zh: 生成的成品也可以在原生 CAD 应用程序中打开。 用户可以查看三维视图，并在文档树中访问创建的 Body、Sketch、Feature、Assembly 和 Component 对象。 文档可以以其原生可编辑格式保存，或导出为标准几何资产，从而保留从智能体生成到人工检查及后续工程工作的路径。

sents.en: The resulting artifact is also available in the native CAD application.
sents.zh: 生成的成品也可以在原生 CAD 应用程序中打开。

paragraphs.en: The interactive loop is supported by an application-level control plane that coordinates agents, tools, resources, permissions, and persistent project state. CAD backends execute domain operations, but they do not decide which agent may act, which calls may run concurrently, or whether an action was based on a current document revision. Keeping these responsibilities in the control plane allows the same orchestration policy to operate across compatible CAD systems.
paragraphs.zh: 交互循环由一个应用级控制平面提供支持，该控制平面协调智能体、工具、资源、权限和持久化项目状态。 CAD 后端执行领域操作，但它们不决定哪个智能体可以行动、哪些调用可以并发运行，或某个动作是否基于当前文档修订版本。 将这些职责保留在控制平面中，可以使同一套编排策略在兼容的 CAD 系统之间通用。

paragraphs.en: For larger projects, a leader agent retains the user conversation and overall goal while delegating bounded subtasks to four built-in roles. The Designer turns functional and geometric intent into a feature and interface plan; the Modeler owns one complete part or a dependency-ordered modeling stage; the Assembler inserts components and manages placements, grounding, mates, and solve state; and the Verifier performs an independent, predominantly read-only evidence pass over the final document and exported assets. Each child receives the original request together with a bounded assignment, separate context, role-specific instructions, tool allowlist, and interaction budget. A child cannot recursively create more agents or modify the leader’s task board. Its final response is returned as evidence together with the resources changed during execution, leaving acceptance and follow-up decisions with the leader.
paragraphs.zh: 对于较大的项目，一个领导智能体会保留用户对话和总体目标，同时将边界明确的子任务委派给四个内置角色。 设计者角色将功能与几何意图转化为特征和接口规划；建模者角色负责一个完整的零件或按依赖顺序排列的建模阶段；装配者角色负责插入组件并管理放置、固定、配合与求解状态；验证者角色则对最终文档和导出的资源执行一次独立的、以只读为主的证据检查。 每个子智能体都会收到原始请求以及一个边界明确的任务分配、独立上下文、角色专属指令、工具允许清单和交互预算。 子智能体不能递归地创建更多智能体，也不能修改领导智能体的任务看板。 其最终回复会作为证据连同执行期间更改的资源一并返回，由领导智能体负责验收和后续决策。

paragraphs.en: Multi-stage work is represented by a compact project task graph. Tasks record their status, description, dependencies, blocking relations, and completion evidence. This graph separates conversational planning from execution state: the leader can recover which components are ready, which assembly step is blocked, and which verification remains after context compaction or session resumption. Dependency updates are serialized by the control plane, preventing two agents from concurrently producing inconsistent task-board transitions.

paragraphs.en: Every tool specification declares static resource behavior, including the arguments that identify reads, writes, observations, creations, or filesystem materialization. Before execution, the resource manager resolves those fields to concrete document, entity, topology, assembly, or file keys. Each agent also maintains the revisions it has actually observed. A write is authorized only when its dependent resources have been observed at their current revisions; if another agent has modified one of them, the stale write is rejected with a recoverable conflict and the agent must inspect the updated state. File edits follow the same rule and require a complete prior read. This observation-based authorization prevents a plausible but outdated model context from silently overwriting newer CAD or project state.

paragraphs.en: Independent child assignments can be emitted together and run concurrently. Tool specifications additionally assign calls to execution lanes and mark them as parallel or exclusive. After resource resolution, write scopes are sorted and locked in a deterministic order; calls with disjoint scopes proceed in parallel, while overlapping CAD writes are serialized. Authorization is revalidated immediately before execution to close the interval between scheduling and dispatch. A successful backend result reports concrete RuntimeResourceEffects ; the control plane commits these effects, advances resource generations, records the responsible agent, and invalidates stale observations held elsewhere. A failed call does not claim a state transition. If transport fails after a potentially mutating call, the affected scope is conservatively invalidated so that later decisions re-inspect it.

This protocol supports useful concurrency without treating the CAD document as an ordinary shared text buffer. Different Modelers may construct independent parts simultaneously, after which an Assembler consumes their committed outputs. Calls that touch the same body, assembly, or output file are ordered, and each downstream agent receives only the document revisions known to be valid at delegation time.

Workspace trust and permission checks are evaluated before protected files or CAD resources are exposed to an agent. The user remains the authority for access that crosses the active project boundary or carries elevated effects. Because permissions are evaluated in the application rather than reimplemented by every backend, adding a CAD integration does not create a second, backend-specific authorization path.

The control plane projects model messages, tool calls, execution outcomes, permissions, resource commits, task changes, and compaction events onto an append-only rollout. The same event stream drives the terminal interface and provides the state required for replay and session restoration. /resume reconstructs an earlier project session, while /compact replaces older interaction with a bounded summary and keeps recent decisions available to the model. Durable memory is extracted from completed root rollouts with links to its source turns, separating persistent design facts from transient dialogue. Skills add reusable CAD procedures, hooks connect project workflows to agent and tool lifecycle events, and a project-level AGENTS.md carries coordinate conventions, naming rules, and delivery requirements into subsequent sessions. Together, these services allow long-running CAD work to remain recoverable, inspectable, and governed by one consistent project state.

The DeciCAD SDK is the contract boundary shared by the application and backend implementations. It defines canonical tool names, typed input and output models, geometry types, opaque object references, permission requirements, runtime resource effects, structured success values, and model-facing errors. The application remains responsible for model interaction, agent orchestration, permissions, sessions, and resource coordination. A backend developer maps the canonical state transitions to the native API of a target CAD system.

This separation makes the SDK a semantic contract rather than a convenience wrapper around one vendor API. Canonical tools are grouped into document, inspection, entity, sketch, solid, and assembly domains. Their Pydantic models normalize units, frames, geometric values, operation modes, and result shapes, while DocumentRef and EntityRef preserve backend-owned object identity as opaque values. A backend imports these specifications instead of copying or redefining them. Consequently, field descriptions, model-facing tool schemas, resource declarations, and output validation remain identical across integrations, while implementation instructions can still describe behavior specific to the target CAD application.

A backend first imports a canonical ToolSpec and binds it to an async implementation with @tool . Inputs have already passed the spec’s Pydantic validation before execution. The implementation returns the canonical output model together with accurate RuntimeResourceEffects ; these effects let the application update resource versions, permissions, and locks. Recoverable CAD failures use a compact ToolError , keeping operational failures distinct from backend defects and transport errors. The backend then declares a manifest containing its backend, SDK, protocol, and tool-contract versions. A BackendServer registers the complete canonical tool roster and exposes a health check for the target CAD runtime, as illustrated in Listing . During activation, a BackendClient starts the isolated process and verifies the manifest, protocol version, tool registry, contract digest, and health response. Only after this initialization does it bind remote executors as ordinary SDK tools inside DeciCAD .
Registering tool domains and exposing backend health through the SDK server.

The server reserves standard output for newline-delimited JSON-RPC frames and sends operational diagnostics to standard error, keeping transport parseable under subprocess supervision. It refuses to initialize when a canonical tool is missing, a tool name is duplicated, an imported spec differs from the SDK, or the manifest targets incompatible SDK, protocol, or tool-contract versions. Successful results are validated against the exact output model before they cross the process boundary; operational failure results contain a ToolError and cannot claim resource effects.

These constraints reduce the work required from a backend developer. The SDK provides model schemas, validation, RPC framing, process lifecycle, contract negotiation, error serialization, and the client-side Tool bindings. The developer concentrates on object resolution, native CAD calls, readiness, and accurate resource effects. A real BackendClient / BackendServer initialization test exercises the same registry and wire contract used by the product, catching integration drift before an agent can invoke the backend. The application and backend may then be released independently whenever their declared contracts remain compatible; an incompatible release fails explicitly at activation instead of producing ambiguous behavior midway through a modeling task.

Our official reference backend instantiates this SDK boundary for FreeCAD, and all experiments in this paper use this backend. The backend manager shown in Figure 14 controls its installation, activation, health checking, update, and removal through an isolated managed environment. In development mode, the setup command also installs a FreeCAD Addon into the versioned user directory discovered from the actual FreeCAD runtime, supporting system, portable, and custom installations.

The integration uses two local communication layers. The SDK BackendClient communicates with an independent backend process; that process connects through an authenticated loopback bridge to FreeCAD’s embedded Python runtime. The bridge executes CAD operations on the FreeCAD GUI thread, wraps document writes in native transactions, and encodes the result under the canonical output model. The bridge panel exposes connection state, dynamic endpoint, protocol version, age of the last authenticated request, and start, stop, restart, and automatic-start controls, while the application sees only the stable SDK contract. Keeping the bridge protocol separate is necessary because FreeCAD owns the embedded interpreter and GUI event loop; it also keeps FreeCAD object lookup, argument decoding, result encoding, transaction handling, and native diagnostics out of the application process.

Stable opaque references connect documents, entities, geometry, topology, features, and assembly objects across calls. Successful tools report concrete resource effects, and failures are mapped into shared error categories, so the general agent and resource runtime do not depend on the FreeCAD Python API.

Inspection is hierarchical rather than a full document dump. Paginated list operations expose document structure and stable references, after which get operations retrieve detailed properties, placement, geometry, topology, or assembly state only for selected objects. Modeling tools return compact native results and resource effects immediately after execution. This supports the same active and passive observation pattern used by the DeciCAD decision loop while retaining direct access to FreeCAD’s editable feature history.

Figure 15 shows a document state produced through this path. The three-dimensional solid is accompanied by its body, additive features, and sketch in the FreeCAD tree, rather than being exposed only as a flattened mesh or image.

For batch evaluation and data collection, multiple workers run isolated FreeCAD and backend processes with separate bridge endpoints, authentication tokens, instance identifiers, and result caches. A worker resets and verifies all open documents before accepting another episode. This isolation prevents CAD state from leaking across tasks while retaining the same backend contract used by the interactive product.

Parallelism is therefore process-isolated rather than implemented by issuing concurrent CAD operations inside one FreeCAD instance. Each worker owns one FreeCAD process, one Addon bridge, and one matching backend process. Distinct endpoint descriptor files lead to independent dynamic loopback ports and authentication tokens. This design supports parallel interactive services, trajectory collection, and benchmark evaluation without sharing mutable FreeCAD state across tasks.

The same SDK contract also supports two commercial CAD systems, SolidWorks and AutoCAD. Each backend declares the capabilities it implements, and the application loads the corresponding tools when it connects; agent orchestration, permissions, resource coordination, and sessions are shared across all backends.
